article_title: Evidence for ESSA: Enhanced Core Reading Instruction (ECRI)
citation: Enhanced Core Reading Instruction. (2017). Evidence review summary. https://www.evidenceforesight.org
title: Tiered reading delivery pattern: 90 minutes whole-group core plus 30 minutes small-group Tier 2 for all struggling readers
description: The studied program used a tiered time structure: "all students, experimental and control, received 90 minutes of core reading instruction and 30 minutes of Tier 2 (supplemental) instruction." Core instruction is whole group with classroom teachers; intervention occurs in small groups of 3-5 students led by teachers or instructional assistants.
requirements: Classroom teachers deliver whole-group core instruction
Teachers or instructional assistants deliver small-group Tier 2 intervention
constraints: The program does not require technology
target_learners: first grade students, including struggling readers
target_learning_goals: foundational reading skills delivered through aligned core and supplemental instruction
examples: In the Oregon and Massachusetts study, both experimental and control students received the same 90-minute core block and 30-minute Tier 2 block.

article_title: Temporal Network Analysis of Collaborative Prototyping from a Knowledge Creation Perspective
citation: Ohsaki, A., Tan, Y., Eagan, B., Shaffer, D. W., & Swiecki, Z. (2026). Temporal Network Analysis of Collaborative Prototyping from a Knowledge Creation Perspective. Journal of Learning Analytics, 13(1), 190–207. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2026.8959
title: Provide timely educator support for concept creation during knowledge creation activities
description: This principle recommends that educators offer timely support to help teams move from information gathering toward concept creation and idea improvement. The article's Notes for Practice states results suggest "supporting concept creation" as a design recommendation for KC learning environments. It is grounded in findings that teams differed in when and whether they reached generative collaborative actions across session phases.
requirements: Educators must monitor team progress through phases to identify when support is needed
constraints: Study did not test an intervention; recommendation is derived from observed differences in team trajectories
target_learners: students unfamiliar with design-mode thinking
higher education students
target_learning_goals: knowledge creation
idea improvement
examples: Service design team continued gathering information in Phase 2 while other teams moved to concept creation, suggesting educators could support teams stuck at information-gathering stages

article_title: Integrating Micro-credentials into Professional Learning: Lessons from Five Districts
citation: Christina Luke and Viki M. Young. (2020). Integrating Micro-credentials into Professional Learning: Lessons from Five Districts. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Tie micro-credentials to district outcomes and redesign professional learning systems around them
description: The report recommends aligning micro-credentials to district goals so teacher time and resources target meaningful student learning outcomes and professional learning is coherent rather than fragmented. Because micro-credentials are competency- and research-based, leaders said they "allow us to track the efectiveness of our PD" and document teachers actually implementing practices, not just sitting through a training.

constraints: Districts may need to renegotiate local collective bargaining agreements and develop school leader buy-in to commit PD time
target_learners: District administrators and K-12 classroom teachers
target_learning_goals: Coherent, goal-aligned professional learning and documented implementation of new practices
examples: One district leader described planning to use micro-credentials for PD in computational thinking and equity, aligned with focus areas the district had already implemented.

title: Use timed readings with caution; build other elements of fluent reading such as automaticity and prosody
description: Although timed readings are common in fluency work, the panel warns against overreliance on speed. "Timed readings can be overused and can be a detriment to student engagement and motivation, especially when used solely to increase reading speed." Instead, fluency-building activities should also target reading effortlessly with automaticity and reading with expression or prosody, using engaging activities that build confidence.

target_learning_goals: Reading with expression, appropriate pacing, and automaticity

title: Let time vary while holding competencies fixed, inverting the traditional fixed-time model

constraints: The brief presents this as a defining feature and contrast, not as a tested effect

target_learning_goals: Demonstration of defined competencies at individually varying pace

article_title: The Teacher Residency: An Innovative Model for Preparing Teachers
citation: Guha, R., Hyler, M.E., and Darling-Hammond, L. (2016). The Teacher Residency: An Innovative Model for Preparing Teachers. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/teacher-residency
title: Integrate coursework tightly with a full-year clinical placement in expert classrooms

Most residents receive at least 900 hours of preservice clinical preparation versus 400-600 hours in traditional programs.

target_learning_goals: Connecting theory and research-based practice to classroom teaching
examples: SFTR residents take night courses tightly integrated with their clinical placement and participate in clinical instructional rounds modeled on medical rounds

article_title: 5 Things for Advocates to Know about Chronic Absenteeism
citation: EdTrust. (2023). 5 Things for Advocates to Know About Chronic Absenteeism. https://EdTrust.org
title: Address chronic absence through tiered prevention and early intervention rather than punishment
description: This principle holds that solving chronic absence requires understanding and addressing the underlying challenges causing students to miss school. The brief states "What works is a tiered response, beginning with universal supports that promote positive conditions of learning and then bolstering with additional interventions that provide more personalized and increasingly intensive interventions, as needed." Such prevention-oriented approaches are described as more effective and less costly than punitive, legal-system-dependent approaches.
requirements: Tiered approach specifics tailored to local realities, challenges, assets, and strengths
Partnering closely with students and families to understand their challenges and strengths
constraints: A cookie cutter approach is much less effective, especially post-pandemic given greater differences in families' economic, social, and health conditions
target_learners: K-12 students at risk of chronic absence
Preschool and kindergarten students
target_learning_goals: Consistent school attendance
Access to classroom instruction and learning conditions
examples: The brief urges school and district leaders to implement locally tailored multi-tiered systems of support to identify and connect students with needed resources, and states to provide guidance and professional development helping districts take a tiered approach.

article_title: Creating Accountability for College Access and Success: Recommendations for the Higher Education Act and Beyond
citation: Kayla C. Elliott, Tiffany Jones. (2016). Creating Accountability for College Access and Success: Recommendations for the Higher Education Act and Beyond. Ed Trust. https://edtrust.org
title: Apply consequences gradually and tiered by infraction, reserving loss of Title IV eligibility for last after support and time have been exhausted
description: The report argues that accountability measures threatening Title IV aid "could cripple or close institutions that enroll high numbers of underserved students," so consequences should be gradual and intermediary first — such as removing tax benefits, program-level targeting, improvement plans, and mandatory alerts — with Title IV elimination only after other steps fail and two years of failing to meet standards.
requirements: Apply consequences and penalties only after the first four principles are pursued and exhausted, and only after two years of failing to meet standards
constraints: The report states campus closures can have the most impact on college opportunity for low-income students and students of color, who already have limited access
target_learners: students from low-income families
students of color
target_learning_goals: protecting college access while enforcing institutional accountability
examples: The report proposes allowing reduced consequences and waivers for institutions showing continual growth rather than punishing progress
key_sources: Kayla C. Elliott, Tiffany Jones. (2016). Creating Accountability for College Access and Success: Recommendations for the Higher Education Act and Beyond. Ed Trust. https://edtrust.org

article_title: Meta-Cognitive Insights into Cognitive Offloading: Mechanisms, Interventions, and Educational Implications
citation: Yufei Guo & Qun Ye. (2026). Meta-cognitive insights into cognitive offloading: mechanisms, interventions, and educational implications. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications. https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-026-06621-5
title: Match feedback type to metacognitive component and task phase: calibrate beliefs before tasks, provide task-specific feedback during tasks
description: The review proposes that feedback interventions should follow "the principle of timing-component matching for feedback interventions": before task commencement, educators should calibrate metacognitive beliefs with accurate, constructive information about individual abilities; during task execution, they should prioritize immediate, specific, task-related feedback such as real-time accuracy indicators. Matching feedback type to the metacognitive component dominant at each stage is said to maximize feedback's positive effects on rational offloading decisions.
requirements: Feedback must be matched to the dominant metacognitive component at each phase — belief-targeting information pre-task, experience-targeting task-specific information during tasks
constraints: Abstract ranking feedback targeting beliefs may fail to affect in-task offloading decisions dominated by metacognitive experiences, as in Grinschgl et al. (2020)
target_learners: students in technology-enhanced learning environments using external cognitive aids
target_learning_goals: rational cognitive offloading decisions and calibrated metacognitive monitoring
examples: The review derives this principle from reconciling Gilbert et al.'s (2020) advice-feedback benefits with Grinschgl et al.'s (2020) null behavioral effect of ranking feedback
key_sources: Yufei Guo & Qun Ye. (2026). Meta-cognitive insights into cognitive offloading: mechanisms, interventions, and educational implications. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications. https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-026-06621-5

article_title: MuTSE: A Human-in-the-Loop Multi-use Text Simplification Evaluator
citation: Rares-Alexandru Roșcan, Gabriel Petre, Adrian-Marius Dumitran, Angela-Liliana Dumitran. (2026). MuTSE: A Human-in-the-Loop Multi-use Text Simplification Evaluator. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.08947
title: Tiered semantic alignment engine with hierarchical embedding fallback and linearity bias heuristic
description: MuTSE's Semantic Alignment Engine visually maps original sentences to their simplified counterparts using a three-tier cascade: a 384-dimensional multilingual transformer embedding (paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2), a hybrid TF-IDF fallback with word- and character-level n-grams, and a tertiary positional fallback. A linearity factor λ penalizes positionally distant alignments via Score(i,j) = CosineSim − |Pos_rel(i) − Pos_rel(j)| × λ, adjustable in real time between 0 and 2 with a default of 0.5. The article describes the linearity bias as "a structural regularizer, effectively offsetting the reduced discriminative capacity inherent to heavily compressed embedding models."
requirements: Sentence embeddings from the multilingual model, with TF-IDF and positional fallbacks for resilience and hardware agnosticism
constraints: The λ default of 0.5 is user-adjustable between 0 and 2; the article notes MT evaluation would require recalibrating λ because cross-lingual syntactic restructuring may not adhere to monotonic sentence order
target_learners: Educators and applied linguists evaluating simplified texts
target_learning_goals: Qualitative evaluation of text simplification for educational purposes
examples: Fig. 2 contrasts pure semantic matching (λ = 0.00) showing scattered, positionally distant alignments with strict positional penalty (λ = 2.00) resolving false positives and enforcing monotonic alignment
key_sources: Rares-Alexandru Roșcan, Gabriel Petre, Adrian-Marius Dumitran, Angela-Liliana Dumitran. (2026). MuTSE: A Human-in-the-Loop Multi-use Text Simplification Evaluator. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.08947

article_title: TibetCPR: A Multimodal Tactile Feedback System to Enhance Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Training in High-Altitude
citation: Yibo Meng, Ruiqi Chen, Zhiming Liu, and Xiaolan Ding. (2026). TibetCPR: A Multimodal Tactile Feedback System to Enhance Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Training in High-Altitude Regions of Tibet. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.07765
title: TibetCPR: a low-cost, self-guided multimodal CPR training system with electrotactile depth feedback, visual rhythm cues, and a Tibetan-language snow-lotus narrative game
description: TibetCPR is "a low-cost, self-guided CPR training system that pairs depth-driven electrotactile feedback with rhythm-driven visual cues within a Tibetan-language narrative." It comprises a wrist-worn electrotactile unit with hydrogel electrodes, a mannequin with an embedded piezoelectric pressure sensor, and a game-UI screen. A deterministic per-compression loop maps peak force to TENS/none/EMS depth signals and running rate to blue/green/red visual states, while correct compressions advance a four-stage snow-lotus blooming sequence that sustains motivation without an instructor.
requirements: Physical chest compression on the mannequin as the sole and primary control input, with all system responses driven directly by real-time compression performance
constraints: Feedback is kept salient but intermittent and boundary-locked, firing only when a compression falls outside the recommended depth range, to avoid overwhelming users during physically demanding compressions
target_learners: CPR-naive lay community members in high-altitude, resource-limited regions, spanning heterogeneous ages, occupations, and educational backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Stable regulation of chest compression depth and rhythm for bystander CPR readiness
examples: Evaluated in a randomised study with 40 lay community members aged 19–56 in the Tibet Autonomous Region, none with prior CPR training
key_sources: Yibo Meng, Ruiqi Chen, Zhiming Liu, and Xiaolan Ding. (2026). TibetCPR: A Multimodal Tactile Feedback System to Enhance Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Training in High-Altitude Regions of Tibet. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.07765

article_title: GenAI Use and GenAI-Assisted Learning Procrastination in University Students: The Roles of Planned Behavior Constructs and Learning GenAI Anxiety
citation: Li Zilin, Huang Jiali, Cui Zhaodi. (2026). GenAI Use and GenAI-Assisted Learning Procrastination in University Students: The Roles of Planned Behavior Constructs and Learning GenAI Anxiety. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071256
title: Treat timely GenAI use as distinct from responsible use, and distinguish deliberate non-use from procrastination
description: The article cautions educators and researchers against equating low GenAI-assisted learning procrastination with good learning. It states that "Lower GALP—that is, more timely use of GenAI—should not be equated with responsible or effective GenAI use", because timely use may reflect habitual or superficial engagement. It also distinguishes procrastination from reasoned avoidance: "Such intentional non-use is qualitatively distinct from procrastination (i.e., delay despite intention)". Designs and measures should therefore capture the intention–behavior gap rather than mere frequency of use.
requirements: Measures of GenAI-related procrastination must capture unnecessary delay despite genuine intention, not general non-use or deliberate avoidance.
constraints: The article's GALP measure did not capture intentional non-use, so the negative use–procrastination association applies only to delay despite intention, not to pedagogically motivated avoidance.
target_learners: university students
target_learning_goals: responsible and timely use of generative AI in learning tasks
examples: The authors note students may deliberately limit or avoid GenAI to cultivate independent problem-solving skills or comply with academic integrity policies, decisions the GALP measure did not capture.
key_sources: Li Zilin, Huang Jiali, Cui Zhaodi. (2026). GenAI Use and GenAI-Assisted Learning Procrastination in University Students: The Roles of Planned Behavior Constructs and Learning GenAI Anxiety. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071256

article_title: The Timing of Learning before Night-Time Sleep Differentially Affects Declarative and Procedural Long-Term Memory Consolidation in Adolescents
citation: Holz J, Piosczyk H, Landmann N, Feige B, Spiegelhalder K, Riemann D, Nissen C, Voderholzer U. (2012). The Timing of Learning before Night-Time Sleep Differentially Affects Declarative and Procedural Long-Term Memory Consolidation in Adolescents. PLoS ONE 7(7): e40963. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0040963
title: Time- and sleep-dependent consolidation: procedural memory consolidates especially effectively when training occurs directly before night-time sleep
description: The article interprets its procedural findings within current models of a time- and sleep-dependent process of motor skill consolidation, in which initially unstable procedural memory representations are especially susceptible to interference in the first hours after training and are strengthened by sleep-specific brain activity. The authors write: "Our observation that motor learning directly before night-time sleep was especially effective fits to current models of a time- and sleep-dependent process of motor skill consolidation." They add that sleep spindles or EEG slow wave activity might foster this consolidation in the procedural memory system.
requirements: A period of night-time sleep occurring within the critical post-learning time window when memory traces are fragile
constraints: The authors note effects might partly reflect circadian phase differences between 3 PM and 9 PM sessions rather than sleep-dependent factors; disentangling would require total-sleep-deprivation control groups
target_learners: Adolescents learning motor skills
target_learning_goals: Procedural (motor skill) memory consolidation
examples: Evening-trained adolescents showed greater finger-tapping speed and accuracy gains than afternoon-trained adolescents at both 24-hour and 7-day retention intervals

article_title: The Psychology and Neuroscience of Curiosity
citation: Kidd, Celeste and Hayden, Benjamin Y. (2015). The psychology and neuroscience of curiosity. Neuron. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2015.09.010
title: Tinbergen's Four Questions as an organizing framework for studying curiosity
description: The article proposes studying curiosity through Tinbergen's Four Questions, which "provide four complementary scientific perspectives on any particular type of behavior". The framework offers four vantage points—function, evolution, mechanism, and development—that allow description of a behavior even when its boundaries are not fully delineated. The authors structure their entire review of curiosity research through this lens, arguing it permits study of information-seeking without first settling a strict definition of curiosity.
requirements: A behavior class whose boundaries are not yet fully delineated can still be described from the four complementary vantage points
constraints: The authors present it as a framework for organizing inquiry, not as a settled taxonomy of curiosity subtypes
target_learners: humans across the lifespan
non-human animals including monkeys, rats, and roundworms
target_learning_goals: understanding the function, evolution, mechanism, and development of curiosity and information-seeking
examples: The review's sections on function, evolution, mechanism, and development each apply one of the four questions to curiosity research

article_title: The Association between Physical Activity During the Day and Long-Term Memory Stability
citation: Pontifex, M. B., Gwizdala, K. L., Parks, A. C., Pfeiffer, K. A. & Fenn, K. M. (2016). The Association between Physical Activity During the Day and Long-Term Memory Stability. Scientific Reports 6, 38148. https://doi.org/10.1038/srep38148
title: Schedule physical activity opportunities so they avoid the 1–2 hours after encoding and fall before retrieval rather than counting total daily activity
description: The article argues that for long-term memory of newly learned declarative material, when activity occurs matters more than how much occurs across the day. Activity roughly 1–2 hours after encoding was "detrimental to the maintenance of information in long-term memory", while activity in the hour before retrieval was associated with greater maintenance. The authors suggest "superior long-term memory of declarative information occurs when physical activity opportunities are more strategically aligned" to fall before encoding or before retrieval.
requirements: Knowledge of when encoding and retrieval occur relative to the schedule of physical activity opportunities
constraints: Findings are cross-sectional and exploratory; the authors state further research is necessary to validate the existence and relative timings of these critical periods, and mechanisms may differ across the lifespan
target_learners: college-aged young adults
target_learning_goals: retention of declarative, paired-associate information over a 12-hour interval
examples: Participants wore heart rate monitors across a 12-hour interval between learning and testing, and sliding-window regressions identified the two critical periods rather than prescribing activity in advance

article_title: A theory-driven reflection on context-aware support for collaborative discussions in light of analytics, affordances, and platforms
citation: Carolyn Rosé, Sanna Järvelä. (2021). A theory-driven reflection on context-aware support for collaborative discussions in light of analytics, affordances, and platforms. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09360-8
title: Theory-driven units of analysis for educational dialogue across multiple timescales
description: The Baker, Schwarz, and Ludvigsen Squib argues for deep theoretical understanding of discussion and its unit of analysis to inform methods for analyzing dialogue over different timescales, from episodes to societal-scale argumentative knowledge construction. The editors summarize: its aim is "to argue for the necessity for a deep, theoretical understanding of discussion and its unit of analysis." It proceeds in three parts: collective thinking enacted through dialogue, critical considerations of timescales, and how timescales are accounted for in units of analysis applied to platform data. General theories of dialogue, cognition, and collective activity guide chosen units of analysis and explain their deep meaning.
requirements: A deep, theoretical understanding of discussion and its unit of analysis before building analysis methods
constraints: Applying it requires viewing collaboration at a societal level over long periods of time, where interactions occur everywhere and nowhere, crossing modalities through multivocal interconnectedness
target_learners: CSCL researchers and designers
students engaging in collaborative dialogue in local and global contexts
target_learning_goals: collective thinking and collaborative knowledge construction
examples: The example of worldwide collaborative knowledge construction about COVID: real differences in perspective, identity-based clashes of practices, in an immense group over a very long period within an ill-defined activity

citation: Heather Toomey Zimmerman, Susan M. Land, Lillyanna Faimon, Yu-Chen Chiu. (2023). article_title: Understanding when anger becomes productive or destructive in collaborative educational games
citation: Taehyun Kim, Mike Tissenbaum. (2025). Understanding when anger becomes productive or destructive in collaborative educational games. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09459-2
title: Tilting in collaborative learning games: anger-driven collapse of group coordination
description: The article adapts the gaming construct of tilt, originally from pinball and esports where it denotes "anger-driven performance collapse," to educational collaborative gameplay. Tilt is defined as a situation where players "experience continuous negative emotions such as anger due to specific events or individuals in the game, leading to impaired decision-making and overall gameplay." In the study, tilt manifested when a student whose ideas were repeatedly rejected disengaged, leaked his team's strategy, and triggered anger spirals that ended productive discourse.
requirements: A collaborative game context where team-level goals and coordination are salient, and anger is typically grounded in teammates' behaviors rather than opponents'.
constraints: The construct is relatively novel in educational research and the authors present it as preliminary insight; once expressions cross impropriety thresholds (e.g., personal attacks) interaction quality can deteriorate rapidly.
target_learners: middle school students (ages 11-14)
target_learning_goals: collaborative discourse and science learning in game-based simulations
examples: Paul, whose alliance proposal was repeatedly rejected, disengaged from his group, told another city 'We will just scam you. Don't trade with us,' and revealed his own group's bidding strategy.
key_sources: Taehyun Kim, Mike Tissenbaum. (2025). Understanding when anger becomes productive or destructive in collaborative educational games. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09459-2

article_title: A temporal network approach to reveal the longitudinal dynamics of CSCL group regulation and productive collaboration
citation: Mohammed Saqr, Sonsoles López-Pernas, Tiina Törmänen. (2026). A temporal network approach to reveal the longitudinal dynamics of CSCL group regulation and productive collaboration. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09464-5
title: Tied duration as a measure of uptake and relevance of regulatory processes
description: Tied duration is the total time an interaction process remains actively receiving responses from the group, computed from the temporal network by aggregating active intervals from first to last uptake, after trimming idle periods. The article uses it as "a temporal measure of its relevance—an improvement over simple frequency counts", feeding weekly tied durations into model-based clustering to identify regulation patterns and into growth models. It quantifies depth of thread discussion rather than treating posts as instantaneous events.
requirements: Timestamped forum data with reply structure so each edge's active interval can be derived from the replied-to and replying posts' timestamps
constraints: The article trims inactivity periods exceeding an idle threshold and treats resumed threads as new episodes unless explicitly continuous
target_learners: higher education students in online problem-based learning groups
target_learning_goals: measuring uptake and relevance of group regulatory processes in collaborative discussions

citation: Ben-Eliyahu, A., & Bernacki, M. L. (2015). Addressing complexities in self-regulated learning: a focus on contextual factors, contingencies, and dynamic relations. Metacognition and Learning, 10, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-015-9134-6
title: A Newell-inspired time-scale taxonomy (cognitive, rational, social bands) for aligning SRL measurement to theorized process duration
description: Adapting Newell's bands taxonomy from cognitive science, the article proposes that SRL phenomena be matched to the time scale at which they are theorized to occur: cognitive-band events over seconds observed with trace methodologies and think-alouds, rational-band events over minutes to hours including strategy changes and motivation fluctuations, and social-band contextual factors enduring over weeks and months. "Combining measures that span more than one band provides a rich account of SRL." Table 1 maps each special-issue study's measures to bands.

title: Time-reversal testing for assessing directional consistency of prospective effects
description: Time-reversal testing, introduced for neuroimaging analysis by Haufe et al. (2013), assesses the Granger-causal strength of prospective effects in noisy contexts. Its rationale is that "since causes must precede effects, reversing the temporal order of a model should result in attenuating or reversing the sign of a prospective effect presumed to be causal", while contemporaneous effects should remain unchanged. The authors adapt it to contrast time-aligned and time-reversed REM variants.
requirements: The time-reversed model must mirror the original model's structure (same lagged and contemporaneous paths, autoregressive structures reversed for both constructs) for commensurability
constraints: Results are compatible with, but do not establish, a causal interpretation; reversing time for only one construct breaks commensurability

target_learning_goals: testing whether observed ASC-ACH lagged patterns are consistent with hypothesized temporal ordering
examples: The authors estimated time-reversed REM variants on Sorjonen et al.'s simulated data and the PALMA data (Fig. 1, B.2 and C.2), with reproducible code in their OSF repository

article_title: The Theory of Immersive Collaborative Learning (TICOL)
citation: Guido Makransky · Gustav Bøg Petersen. (2023). The Theory of Immersive Collaborative Learning (TICOL). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09822-5
title: TICOL: a theory of immersive collaborative learning organized around four psychological factors
description: TICOL is a theoretical framework describing how collaboration through head-mounted-display immersive media differs from collaboration through traditional systems such as laptops. It proposes that technological features, social affordances, and pedagogical techniques foster four psychological factors—social presence, physical presence, body ownership, and agency—which the authors hypothesize influence the quality of cognitive and socio-emotional social interaction, the social space, and ultimately learning outcomes through ten hypothesized paths. The article states: "In TICOL, we propose that technological features, social affordances, and pedagogical techniques can foster four psychological factors that we define as fundamentally different in XRCL compared to collaboration that occurs through traditional systems (e.g., laptops)". TICOL builds on CSCL frameworks (Kreijns et al.), collaborative cognitive load theory, the immersion principle in multimedia learning, and CAMIL.
requirements: XRCL environments accessed through head-mounted displays, where two or more people interact via avatars with the objective of learning
constraints: The authors state XRCL research is in its infancy and present TICOL as hypotheses to be empirically challenged and built on, not tested predictions
target_learners: distributed learners collaborating across locations, e.g., higher education students
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge construction and co-construction of knowledge and skills
examples: The framework is illustrated with examples such as co-constructing an enlarged virtual cell during a virtual tour through the human bloodstream, and the Engage VR meet-and-greet high-five affordance

article_title: Supporting parents to support children: A U.K. randomized controlled trial testing a text message intervention to cultivate the home learning environment.
citation: O'Reilly, F., Loeb, S., Farrell, A., & Scerif, G. (2026). Supporting Parents to Support Children: A U.K. Randomized Controlled Trial Testing a Text Message Intervention to Cultivate the Home Learning Environment. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000973
title: Tips by Text: a 12-month FACT/TIP/GROWTH text message program for parents of reception children
description: Tips by Text is a 12-month text messaging intervention for parents of Reception students aged 4–5 years, adapted from a U.S. program and delivered through schools' existing texting platforms. Each week parents received three messages: a FACT message with information about the targeted skill, a TIP message with a practical activity using common household objects, and a GROWTH message reinforcing long-term benefits. The article reports that "The split of content was 50% language and early literacy, 25% socioemotional skill development, and 25% numeracy." Fidelity was high, with 81% of treatment parents receiving at least 150 of 165 messages.
requirements: Parents' telephone numbers shared by schools and entered into a texting platform; messages delivered on a fixed weekly schedule
constraints: Messages were sent in English, which the article notes may have reduced effectiveness for non-English-speaking parents; parents received no responses from the research team
target_learners: Parents of 4- to 5-year-old reception students in England
target_learning_goals: Children's language, literacy, numeracy, and socioemotional skills via enriched home learning interactions
examples: In the trial, messages were sent at 3.45 p.m. on Mondays and Wednesdays and 10.30 a.m. on Saturdays, timings chosen after two rounds of piloting with parents and teachers

article_title: Explaining forgetting at different timescales requires a time-variant forgetting function
citation: Maarten van der Velde, Florian Sense, Jelmer P. Borst & Hedderik van Rijn. (2026). Explaining forgetting at different timescales requires a time-variant forgetting function. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00447-1
title: Time-variant forgetting parameters within ACT-R as an explanatory framework for retention across timescales
description: The article proposes letting ACT-R declarative-memory parameters vary with the between-session interval instead of assuming one fixed forgetting function. Three candidate mechanisms are offered: a retrieval threshold (τ) governing the minimum activation needed for retrieval, a decay rate (d) quantifying how quickly traces weaken, and a scaling factor (h) capturing contextual interference by shrinking between-session time. The authors note that "the same observations of response accuracy on a retrieval task can be explained through any one of these three mechanisms," and that a declining threshold suggests increasing retrieval effort, time-variant decay fits consolidation accounts, and decreasing h reflects declining interference.
requirements: A behavioural measure of response accuracy on retrieval trials across a wide range of between-session intervals to fit the parameters per interval bin
constraints: Response accuracy alone cannot identify which of the three parameters drives the fit; including response time would be needed to separate activation-related parameters (d and h) from the threshold (τ)
ACT-R makes no explicit predictions about whether or how each parameter should vary across timescales
target_learners: undergraduate students using adaptive fact-learning systems
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of factual course material through retrieval practice
examples: Fitting threshold, decay, and scaling parameters separately to logarithmically spaced interval bins of naturalistic fact-learning data
key_sources: Maarten van der Velde, Florian Sense, Jelmer P. Borst & Hedderik van Rijn. (2026). Explaining forgetting at different timescales requires a time-variant forgetting function. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00447-1

citation: Alvarez, N., Sanchez-Ruiz, A., Cavazza, M., Shigematsu, M., & Prendinger, H. (2014). Narrative Balance Management in an Intelligent Biosafety Training Application for Improving User Performance. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25, 35–59. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0022-z
title: Integrate narrative with learning content so that narrative events generate the training tasks themselves
description: The article argues that narrative elements should not be an independent layer added on top of training mechanics, but should be the mechanism that generates events and tasks: "we use narrative techniques to generate the events in the scenario, giving to the user new tasks to solve or helping him", so the events directly determine the type and number of training contents experienced. This follows the article's reading of prior work that engagement raises knowledge acquisition when educational content and narrative are motivationally and tightly integrated. Balancing difficulty is also framed as a route toward psychological flow, keeping learners interested.
requirements: A task model database mapping domain tasks so narrative-triggered events correspond to genuine training content
constraints: The article notes prior work found off-task possibilities within narratives can hinder user performance, and results on engagement-to-learning links have been controversial
target_learners: Students in virtual training environments for procedural protocols
target_learning_goals: Engagement and persistence in training
Learning outcomes for safety protocols
examples: In Bio-safety Lab the Narrative Manager creates new spills, hides tools, or gives hints, and these events are themselves the practice content the user must resolve

citation: Kochmar, E., Vu, D. D., Belfer, R., Gupta, V., Serban, I. V., & Pineau, J. (2022). Automated Data-Driven Generation of Personalized Pedagogical Interventions in Intelligent Tutoring Systems. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 32, 323–349. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00267-x
title: Three-tier personalization architecture for feedback selection in a dialogue-based ITS
description: The article organizes feedback selection as three increasingly personalized Random Forest models: a BASELINE model using only "linguistic features" assessing hint quality in isolation (14 features), a SHALLOW PERSONALIZATION model adding 8 "performance-based features" such as past attempts and correctness proportions (22 total), and a DISCOURSE PERSONALIZATION model that also analyzes up to 4 previous interaction turns with keyword, topic-overlap, and perplexity features (49 total). Models are trained in a binary classification setting to predict whether a student will correctly solve the exercise on the next attempt given a hint. This architecture lets an ITS choose pedagogical interventions without hand-crafted rules.
requirements: A database of expectations (reference solutions) from which hints are generated, and recorded historical student–system interactions for training
constraints: The number of previous dialogue turns (up to 4) was selected to maximize coverage of interactions available on the platform at the time of the experiments
target_learners: adult online learners of machine learning and data science
target_learning_goals: problem-solving exercises in data science and machine learning
examples: The three models were compared on 50-fold cross-validation and in the live pilot, with the discourse model winning in both

citation: Alshehri, M., Alamri, A., Cristea, A. I., & Stewart, C. D. (2021). Towards Designing Profitable Courses: Predicting Student Purchasing Behaviour in MOOCs. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 31, 215–233. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00246-2

description: Because time spent on each step proved a powerful predictor of purchasing behaviour, the article recommends that course designers treat increasing time spent on the platform as a design goal. The authors write that "increasing time spent on the MOOC platform is a desirable target for course designers" and that this can be refined "by targeting different adaptive strategies based on the learners' characteristics". constraints: Time as a prediction variable is controversial on online platforms due to potential influence by external variables; the study did not experimentally test whether increasing time spent causes purchasing

target_learning_goals: Course design that supports purchasing behaviour and platform sustainability

citation: Wanzek, J., Vaughn, S., Scammacca, N., Gatlin, B., Walker, M. A., & Capin, P. (2016). Meta-analyses of the effects of tier 2 type reading interventions in grades K-3. Educational Psychology Review, 28, 551-576.
title: Implement early-grade Tier 2 reading support as less extensive interventions delivered 1:1 or in small groups of five or fewer students, by varied implementers.
description: The meta-analysis supports delivering supplemental (15-99 session) reading intervention to K-3 students with or at risk for reading difficulties either one-on-one or in small groups of five or fewer, since effects did not differ across these group sizes and school personnel implemented interventions as effectively as researchers. The summary states "the research supports intervention provided 1:1 and in small groups of five or fewer students," and that interventions "can be feasibly implemented by a variety of implementers."

constraints: Only one-to-one and small groups (2-3 or 4-5 students) could be examined; only three studies used larger groups, so no conclusion covers groups larger than five.

target_learning_goals: foundational reading skills (phonological awareness, phonics, word recognition, fluency)
language and reading comprehension
examples: Across the 72 studies, interventions were delivered 1:1 or in groups of 2-3 or 4-5 students by researchers, general education teachers, special education teachers, and paraprofessionals, with no significant differences in effects by implementer or group size.

students from secondary school to university

data analysis and inference from random experiments

citation: National Foundation for Educational Research (NFER), evaluation team led by Simon Rutt. (2014). Catch Up® Numeracy: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/evaluation
title: Plan structured one-to-one interventions into the school timetable from the start of the year to secure delivery priority
description: The evaluation's key conclusions recommend that structured interventions be given protected space in the school timetable from the outset. constraints: Schools found it challenging to run two 15-minute sessions per week due to timetabling and other issues; pupil and staff absences further reduced delivered sessions

target_learning_goals: numeracy skills
examples: In the trial, sessions were held at varied times including registration, assembly, lunch and afternoon lessons; only around half of schools had a policy about when interventions should be run, and ring-fenced time was not commonplace.

description: The article invokes the time-based resource-sharing model as the explanatory account connecting processing speed to working memory performance. title: Time Utilization Theory as the framework linking commuting time to academic and mental-health outcomes
description: The article applies Time Utilization Theory, proposed by John P. Robinson in 1980, to explain how commuting time affects student outcomes. The theory "highlights the consequential effects of time allocation on behavioral patterns and psychological health" and is "frequently employed to examine how individuals prioritize and allocate their time across different activities". In this study, longer commutes are theorized to impose time constraints that crowd out sleep and outdoor activity, which in turn harm academic performance and mental health; the mediation results are interpreted through this lens.
requirements: Requires measurement of how individuals allocate time across activities such as sleep, study, and leisure to trace the mechanism.
constraints: The article notes previous research on commuting effects has yielded inconsistent findings, which it attributes to methodological limitations including small samples and insufficient consideration of confounding variables.
target_learners: Rural primary school students (grades 4-5) in northwest China
target_learning_goals: Academic performance in mathematics
Mental health (general anxiety)
examples: The study tests three time-allocation channels: sleep time, after-school outdoor activity time, and after-school study time, finding the first two significantly reduced by commuting.
